Harmonic Ratio

GeometryConstructionsFractions
Game: Join five moving dots with straight lines to pin down a spot called D that will not budge.
How to play: Drag a dot, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Check the ratio to see what stays fixed, and Show names to turn the letters on or off.
Look for the math

Here is a drawing that keeps its promise. Move almost any dot and the lines change completely, yet the point D on the line AB lands in exactly the same place.

Building with straight lines

Start with A, B and C in a row. Choose E off the line and I on AE. Draw CE and BI; they cross at G. Draw AG; it meets EB at F. Draw IF; it meets AB at D. Only a straightedge is needed. The applet also computes H where CE meets ID, though it does not draw it; this page shows H as a small dot.

The archived page says it takes six more lines than AB to obtain point C. Counting the applet's own lines gives five — CE, IB, AG, EB and IF — and the point they produce is D. The logic test records that slip; the construction here follows the applet.

Where D lands

Put a coordinate on the line with A = 0 and B = 1, and let C = u. Solving the construction gives D = u / (2u - 1). When C lies between A and B, D lies outside the segment, on the far side of B. The logic test tried 4,200 pairs of choices for E and I and found the same D every time, to within a few ten-thousandths of a pixel.

This is a different idea from the site's Harmonic Mean page: that page builds a length 2ab/(a+b) with angle bisectors. Here the connection is that AB is the harmonic mean of the lengths AC and AD — 2/AB = 1/AC + 1/AD.

Why D cannot move

The tool is the cross-ratio, a number attached to four points on a line. The page defines (ABCD) = CA/CB : DA/DB, using signed lengths. Looking from E, the lines to A, B, C, D meet AB at those same four points, and they also meet the lines through I, F, H, D at A, B, C, D. So (ABCD) = E(ABCD) = E(IFHD) = (IFHD). Looking from G gives (IFHD) = G(IFHD) = G(BACD) = (BACD).

Swapping the first two letters turns a cross-ratio upside down, so (ABCD) = 1/(BACD). Together those equations force (ABCD)² = 1, and the order of the points makes it negative: (ABCD) = -1. Four points with this value are called harmonic conjugates. The test checked all four of these equalities on thousands of diagrams.

Three conjugate pairs

The four lines CE, IB, AG and EB form a complete quadrilateral. Its diagonal points come in conjugate pairs: C and D with respect to A and B, H and D with respect to I and F, and C and H with respect to E and G. This is the pole and polar story in a straightedge-only form. If two lines are nearly parallel the applet's own intersection routine gives no point at all; the page refuses to claim a theorem in that case.

Try dragging C very close to halfway between A and B. D rushes off one end of the line, then comes back from the other end.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
